abstract: Chromosome-scale genome sequences from across the barley genus Hordeum reveal large structural variation, evidence of ancient genetic exchange and extensive divergence of regulatory sequences. These evolutionary processes have generated diversity that could be used to improve cultivated barley. Genome sequences across Hordeum reveal conserved chromosome ends and coding genes, but divergent chromosome centres and regulatory DNA.
title: A fine-grained reconstruction of barley’s evolutionary history

abstract: Australian migratory moths navigate long distances, in part owing to a stellar ‘compass’. It transpires that they have another compass that detects the inclination, or angle, of Earth’s magnetic field lines and that probably relies on a light-dependent quantum-mechanical mechanism similar to the one found in night-migratory songbirds. Migratory moths distinguish poleward from equatorward by sensing the inclination of magnetic field lines.
title: Bogong moths can migrate using an internal geomagnetic compass

abstract: Drought is a major environmental constraint limiting global crop production 1 , 2 . On average, crop productivity typically declines by 30–40% in moderate-drought years, whereas extreme droughts trigger far greater reductions 3 , 4 . As droughts become longer and more intense due to climate change, adverse effects on crop productivity are expected to escalate 5 . Breaking the trade-offs between stress resistance and yield is key to advancing crop genetic improvement as climate change sets in and the world population grows, but this is challenging for drought stress 6 . Here we show that heterologous expression of EpTFIIAγ , a gene encoding a transcription factor induced by osmotic stress in an extremophile lichen mycobiont, partially decouples trade-offs between stress resistance and grain production, enhancing plot yields of five wheat cultivars under water deficit by 19.4–32.8%, and per-plant yields of rice and maize by 19.7–42.4% in the greenhouse and multiple field environments. EpTFIIAγ physically interacts with endogenous transcriptional activators to synergistically enhance both stress-responsive and developmental transcriptional programs, simultaneously boosting photosynthetic capacity and water-use efficiency, while delaying senescence via multiple physiological and developmental enhancements, ultimately increasing grain yields. EpTFIIAγ uncouples antagonistic stress-response and biomass production pathways in multiple crops and delivers a straightforwards and broad-spectrum strategy for sustainably improving staple-crop yields regardless of water availability.
title: An extremophile transgene improves drought resistance and yield in cereals

abstract: CRISPR-associated transposases (CASTs) achieve site-specific DNA integration by combining the RNA-guided targeting action of a nuclease-deficient CRISPR–Cas system with the assembly of a Tn7-like transpososome complex 1,2. Understanding the detailed mechanisms of this elaborate process is paramount to engineering CAST systems into programmable genetic tools 3–6. Type I-F Pseudoalteromonas CAST (Pse CAST) shows the highest activity in mammalian cells so far 7 and has been adapted extensively through directed evolution 8. However, its continued rational engineering requires addressing critical gaps in our understanding of transpososome assembly and activation 9. Here we perform structural analyses using cryogenic electron microscopy, validated by DNA transposition assays, to visualize the Pse CAST system in a series of functional states that define the stepwise mechanism of RNA-guided DNA integration. The structures of the Pse CAST targeting and transposase recruitment complexes revealed that conformational changes in the Cascade–TniQ module, induced by R-loop formation, are associated with target-DNA stabilization and TnsC heptamerization. This, in turn, results in the recruitment of the TnsAB transposase by conserved interactions with the carboxy-terminal tail of TnsB. Finally, the structure of the 1.2 MDa Pse CAST transpososome holocomplex revealed allosteric coupling of TnsC–TnsB and TnsB–target-DNA interactions to the conformational remodelling of the TnsB catalytic site, activating donor-DNA integration. Together, these findings establish a unified mechanistic blueprint for RNA-guided DNA integration by type I CASTs and provide a structural framework to guide their engineering for genome-editing applications.
title: Structural basis of RNA-guided DNA integration by type I CAST systems

abstract: Although coronary artery disease (CAD) genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified hundreds of loci, most variants lie in non-coding regions, obscuring the causal gene programmes and cell types driving disease 1 , 2 . Here we performed single-nucleus multi-omic profiling of gene expression and chromatin accessibility in human coronary arteries from 44 people to construct a genome-wide single-cell variant-to-enhancer-to-gene map. We identified 11,269 chromatin accessibility quantitative trait loci (caQTLs) across principal vascular cell types, including CAD-associated caQTLs in smooth muscle cells (SMCs). Using dynamic single-cell caQTL modelling 3 , we show that variant effects on chromatin vary across SMC states. For example, rs658956 -mediated suppression of the FGGY-DT enhancer through disruption of an AP-1 motif is amplified as SMCs transition towards a fibromyocyte fate. We next performed genome-wide high-throughput chromosome conformation capture (Hi-C) in 15 human coronary arteries, showing that rs4887091 in the ADAMTS7 CAD locus has allele-dependent effects on CCCTC-binding factor occupancy and loop strength. Integrating Hi-C, Hi-C with chromatin immunoprecipitation and in vitro clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats interference (CRISPRi) nominated AMOTL2 as a distal SMC-specific CAD gene whose loss promotes proliferation and suppresses contractile identity. Finally, arrayed Perturb–seq of GWAS-nominated enhancers converged on extracellular matrix remodelling as a core SMC disease programme. Together, these findings provide a framework for mapping non-coding GWAS variants to cell types, chromatin states and gene programmes in human disease.
title: Single-cell variant-to-enhancer-to-gene map for coronary artery disease

abstract: Colloidal quantum dot solids are promising for photoconversion and photochemistry, but their performance is fundamentally limited by rapid hot-carrier cooling, low carrier mobility and short transport ranges 1 . Here we demonstrate a spin-exchange-driven phototransport regime in manganese-doped quantum dot films that enables the generation, long-range transport and regeneration of hot carriers. Ultrafast spin-exchange-mediated Auger upconversion promotes electrons into high-energy, delocalized states before phonon cooling 2 , 3 , establishing a transient high-mobility conduction channel. Crucially, spin-exchange interactions not only generate hot carriers but also enable their repeated re-excitation, thereby sustaining long-range drift. This mechanism yields room-temperature mobilities of about 150 cm 2 V −1 s −1 and submillimetre drift lengths—far greater than those of conventional quantum dot solids and approaching values characteristic of crystalline semiconductors. Time-of-flight measurements confirm drift-dominated transport, with transit times scaling linearly with distance and inversely with electric field. These results establish a route to long-range energy transport in nanoscale materials and enable the use of hot carriers in photoconversion, photochemistry and transit-time-limited photodetection.
title: Submillimetre hot-electron transport in manganese-doped quantum dot solids

abstract: Precise genomic integration of large DNA cargo remains a central challenge in genome engineering. CRISPR-associated transposases (CASTs) 1 , 2 offer a promising solution by coupling RNA-guided DNA recognition to transposon-mediated integration. Because of their exceptional targeting fidelity, type I-F3 CASTs have been a major research focus 1 , yet the structural basis of their RNA-guided DNA integration has remained unclear. Here, using cryo-electron microscopy, computational protein design and functional assays, we report the licensing mechanisms that control DNA integration activity of Vibrio cholerae CAST (VchCAST). Structural determination was enabled by zero-shot computational redesign of TnsA, which enhanced integration activity by nearly two orders of magnitude without compromising specificity. The structure of the holo integration complex reveals the conformational licensing events that govern activation of the integration machinery at the on-target site. Multiple components (Cascade–TniQ, TnsC and TnsA–TnsB) undergo conformational changes upon assembly into the holo integration complex, and the catalytically competent state is stabilized only within the full assembly. Comparison with existing CAST integration complex structures reveals conserved architectural features, suggesting a common molecular basis for RNA-guided transposition across CASTs. Our findings establish a general mechanistic framework for RNA-guided DNA integration and demonstrate that protein design is a powerful strategy for engineering highly active CAST systems.
title: Licensing mechanisms during RNA-guided DNA integration by type I-F3 CAST

abstract: Intratumoural heterogeneity, originating from genetic, epigenetic and phenotypic diversity, is pervasive in cancer and a fundamental barrier to curative treatment 1,2. How these heterogeneous cell states emerge and co-evolve within tumours remains poorly understood. Here we develop a deep-learning framework that quantifies colorectal cancer tissue architecture and nuclear morphology at subcellular resolution to predict patient outcome. Integrating this with spatial transcriptomics, multiplex immunofluorescence and patient-derived organoids, we identify a co-evolutionary relationship between tumour architecture and cancer cell states. We identify architectural interfaces in colorectal cancer that drive cell state diversification by promoting distinct cancer stem cell programmes. Specifically, tissue fragmentation generates compressive forces that activate YAP, suppressing classical stem cell programmes and inducing fetal/regenerative stem cell states that initially manifest as hybrid states with features of partial epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT). Subsequent tumour–stroma communication through TGFβ diversifies these into distinct stem cell and EMT states. Reciprocally, β-catenin activity tunes tumour cell responsiveness to architectural cues. Collectively, this work identifies a feedforward loop between cell states and tissue architecture that drives cancer heterogeneity and cell state diversification. Machine-learning-based analyses harness this co-dependency, independently of mutational status or cancer stage, to predict patient outcome.
title: Heterogeneity co-evolves with architecture to determine colon cancer outcome

abstract: Heterochromatin typically represses genes 1,2, yet some genes paradoxically require it for activation 3–7. How can the same chromatin environment both silence and promote transcription? Here we address this question by interrogating the clustered protocadherin (Pcdh) locus, where subsets of genes are stochastically expressed while most remain silent 8. In neurons, stochastic and combinatorial expression of Pcdh genes generates unique cell-surface barcodes required for self–non-self discrimination and neural circuit assembly 8. By combining RNA labelling of Pcdh genes and neurodevelopmental cell types with single-molecule chromatin tracing and stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy, we find that a compact heterochromatin domain containing Pcdh genes forms as these genes become activated during development. Pcdh transcription occurs within the compact domain and reads through downstream genes, and distal enhancers must access the domain to engage target promoters. Genetic perturbations in mice suggest that opposing genome folding forces cooperate to establish Pcdh locus architecture and promote stochastic Pcdh expression. Specifically, while DNA loop extrusion allows enhancers to breach heterochromatin and find target promoters, heterochromatin-driven compartmentalization supports an expanded enhancer–promoter search space. These findings shed light on a process foundational to the development of vertebrate nervous systems and suggest a mechanism for how transcription can occur within seemingly silent chromatin environments.
title: Transcription from megabase-scale heterochromatin generates neural barcodes

abstract: Cancer-associated mutations in PIK3CA underlie congenital overgrowth disorders that frequently involve the vasculature1,2. Among the affected tissues, the endothelium commonly exhibits aberrant expansion, leading to vascular malformations3. Notably, these lesions arise predominantly in veins and capillaries, whereas arteries are largely spared, for reasons that remain unclear. Here, using genetic lineage tracing, we show that endothelial expression of PIK3CAH1047R drives profound clonal expansion of capillary and venous endothelial cells, whereas mature arterial endothelial cells are refractory to pathological PI3K activation. Expression of PIK3CAH1047R in arterial precursors disrupts arterial differentiation and promotes the acquisition of venous features, providing a mechanistic explanation for the paucity of arterial lesions after PIK3CA genetic perturbation. Mechanistically, these effects are mediated by two complementary downstream branches of PI3K signalling: increased proliferation, which drives vascular overgrowth, and upregulation of the venous-specifying transcription factor NR2F2 (also known as COUP-TFII), which suppresses arterial differentiation. Together, our findings reveal that pathogenic responses to PIK3CAH1047R are dictated by endothelial differentiation state and fate trajectory, and demonstrate that arterial endothelium is intrinsically resistant to oncogenic PI3K signalling. Arteries are therefore shielded from PIK3CA mutations, explaining the rarity of arterial malformations in PIK3CA-driven disease. Expression of PIK3CAH1047R in arterial precursors disrupts arterial differentiation and promotes the acquisition of venous features.
title: Context-dependent response of endothelial cells to PIK3CA mutation

abstract: Molecular and morphological evidence increasingly supports the view that most East Asian Middle to Late Pleistocene archaic Homo belong to Denisovans 1 , yet the presence of other contemporaneous lineages has remained unclear. Here we report a set of newly discovered hominin fossils (4 isolated teeth; more than 100.8 thousand years ago and 104.5–42.6 thousand years ago, respectively) from 2 cave sites (Chuanshandong and Longchuandong) in Guangxi, southern China. Integrated morphological and palaeoproteomic analyses reveal substantial phenotypic and molecular diversity consistent with at least two distinct lineages. One lineage (Longchuandong) is assigned to a Denisovan-affinity population, owing to its extreme similarity to Altai Denisovans with respect to dental morphology and single amino acid polymorphisms that match those of Denisovans from Harbin, Penghu, Bianfu Cave and Altai. The other lineage, represented by the Chuanshandong hominin, is an unresolved archaic Homo , as it carries an ancestral variant (AMELY 179M) shared with Homo antecessor and great apes and another variant (AMBN 253G) that is diagnostic of East Asian Middle Pleistocene Homo erectus but lacks the Denisovan-associated AMBN 273V variant (it being highly probable that this is inherited from H. erectus ). Dental morphology in this lineage exhibits a mosaic of plesiomorphic and derived traits but no clear Denisovan affinity. These findings indicate that diverse hominin populations may have inhabited subtropical China during the Middle and Late Pleistocene, including a Denisovan-affinity population and another unresolved archaic Homo .
title: Middle–Late Pleistocene Denisovans and unresolved Homo in southern China

abstract: Highly heritable, polygenic and easily measured, adult height has long been the model trait in human genetics 1 , 2 . Although the landscape of height-associated common genetic variation has been studied extensively 2 , rare variation remains relatively unexplored 1 . Here, using rare protein-altering variants in a discovery set of 826,066 exomes, we identify 207 height-associated genes, 98% of which replicate in an additional 624,567 individuals. The rarest and most deleterious class of variation, singleton (frequency < 0.0001%) putative loss-of-function variants, implicated 17 genes with large effects on height ranging from −17cm ( ACAN ) to +11 cm ( FBN1 ) per allele, 52× larger than the average effect of common height-associated variants and comparable to the 1% tails of a common variant polygenic score. Several genes ( TET1 , DTL and IGF2BP2 ) have effect sizes that are at least as large as established Mendelian height genes, yet lack documented stature or skeletal growth syndromes, particularly for genes associated with increased height. Our large-scale sequencing study elucidates the genetic architecture and allelic heterogeneity of rare variants in height, providing unique insights into their large effects—often similar to or larger than recognized Mendelian syndromes—and their impact on trait prediction, clinical evaluation, and discovery power to facilitate drug target prioritization.
title: Rare-variant genetic architecture of height in over 1.4 million individuals

abstract: Climate change and disturbances are reshaping forest ecosystems worldwide 1–4, yet their combined effects on species redistribution remain poorly understood. Here we analyse repeated measurements from 44,368 forest inventory plots spanning 1999–2025, with an average remeasurement interval of 10 years, to examine how climate and natural disturbances jointly influence the elevational redistribution of tree species across the western USA. We show that climate warming increased sapling abundance, whereas increasing drought frequency and recent natural disturbances (fire, insect outbreaks and disease) reduced tree abundance, particularly among adult trees. By contrast, legacy fire was associated with increased sapling abundance, with stronger positive responses in angiosperms than in gymnosperms. These influences were distributed unevenly across species’ elevational ranges: upper portions of species’ ranges generally experienced stronger warming, greater increases in drought frequency and more disturbance activity than lower portions, creating elevational asymmetries in stress and recovery. These elevational asymmetries were associated with more pronounced downslope shifts in basal area centres, probably reflecting disturbance effects on larger trees. By contrast, stem abundance centres showed more divergent shifts, consistent with sapling responses to both climate change and disturbance. Our findings reveal contrasting demographic responses to climate change and natural disturbances that shape the elevational redistribution of different species, with potential consequences for forest composition, resilience and long-term stability.
title: Disturbances and climate drive tree elevational shifts

abstract: The abundances of stable isotopes in methane (CH 4) are used to distinguish fossil and biological emissions and to constrain the global methane budget. While these analyses require correction for isotopic fractionation occurring in methane’s atmospheric reactions, the temperature dependence of the kinetic isotope effects (KIEs) are poorly described and typically ignored. Here we combine density functional theory, Møller–Plesset perturbation theory, coupled-cluster calculations, and tunneling-corrected transition state theory to develop a first-principles description of the temperature-dependent KIEs for CH 4 and its isotopologues reacting with OH and Cl over the range 100 to 500 K which exhibit substantial and previously neglected temperature dependence. Incorporation of these KIEs into the EMAC chemistry–climate model yields systematically different effective atmospheric sink fractionation factors than those obtained using temperature-invariant values. The largest differences occur for chlorine oxidation in the cold upper troposphere and stratosphere, where methane isotope budgets are particularly sensitive to reactive halogens. We find a weak 13 C–D clumping anomaly and a strong D–D clumping anomaly, confirming earlier work and demonstrating that atmospheric oxidation produces substantial enrichment in Δ 12 CH 2 D 2, and helping to reconcile source signatures with atmospheric observations. These results show that temperature-dependent KIEs are required for robust interpretation of methane isotopes in both contemporary and past atmospheres.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Temperature-dependent kinetic isotope effects in methane reactions with OH and Cl reshape atmospheric sink fractionation

abstract: Ice uniquely provides direct samples of ancient atmosphere, enabling measurements of greenhouse gases contemporaneous to temperature reconstructions. Blue ice areas (covering 1% of the surface of Antarctica) hold a largely underexplored paleoclimate record that can extend beyond deep ice cores (that is, older than 1.5 My), covering periods in which global surface temperatures were similar to projected future temperatures. Blue ice areas expose ancient ice directly at the surface or at shallow depths due to net ablation and redirected ice flow, providing access to old ice at logistically reduced costs. However, the analysis and interpretation of blue ice samples is challenging, given the complex flow patterns in these regions that result in tilted layers, inversions and discontinuities in the stratigraphy, and complex ice–bedrock interactions. This paper presents a succinct review of state-of-the-art blue ice research, placed in the context of established ice core research, and argues that to advance the search for ancient ice, efforts in blue ice areas should focus on: i) collecting dated surface samples, ii) investigating the relationship between the age of the ice and other datable evidence, such as moraines, dust layers, meteorites, and exposed bedrock, and iii) developing models that can capture the typically disturbed or discontinuous stratigraphy. Together with advances in analytical techniques that address, for example, contamination and absolute dating, these efforts could lead to the recovery of the oldest ice on Earth, unravel warm climates of the past, and improve future climate change projections.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Unlocking the unparalleled paleoclimate record of Antarctic blue ice areas

abstract: We describe a severe MEFV -associated autoinflammatory disease, distinct from familial Mediterranean fever (FMF), and designate it CHIVE-18 syndrome (Compound Heterozygosity for I692del and V726A MEFV variants and Elevated IL-18). We present the clinical features and inflammatory signatures of 44 CHIVE-18 patients and 9 other patients with two MEFV variants including I692del. Clinical findings in CHIVE-18 patients often include transfusion-dependent anemia, arthritis, organomegaly, inflammatory bowel disease, failure to thrive, and less frequently cytokine storm, Amyloid A (AA) amyloidosis, and neutrophilic dermatoses. Serum total and free IL-18 levels in CHIVE-18 patients were markedly elevated compared to those of healthy controls, classical FMF patients, and compound heterozygotes for I692del and a pathogenic MEFV variant other than V726A and were comparable to the previously described levels of patients with pyogenic arthritis, pyoderma gangrenosum, and acne syndrome. Cultured U937 cells expressing the V726A/I692del double mutant exhibited significantly increased release of IL-1β, IL-18, and lactate dehydrogenase compared to the other FMF-associated mutants. Patients’ myeloid cells showed enhanced STAT1 phosphorylation after stimulation with IFNγ. Despite having undetectable serum IL-1β, a previously reported CHIVE-18 patient with autoimmune hepatitis had in situ staining of a liver biopsy that showed high expression of IL-1β, TNFα, and IL-18, which localized to CD68+ tissue macrophages. CHIVE-18 patients usually require an IL-1 inhibitor and sometimes combination therapy with another biologic to control disease activity. In summary, CHIVE-18 is a distinct, severe disease that expands the spectrum of MEFV -associated autoinflammatory disorders and highlights genotype/phenotype complexity in compound heterozygous disorders.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Compound heterozygosity for I692del and V726A variants in MEFV leads to severe autoinflammation and elevated interleukin-18 (CHIVE-18)

abstract: Since the earliest artificial gears, parallel gearbox systems based on intermeshing two-dimensional (2D) networks of multiple gear units have served a fundamental role in macroscale mechanical devices through the correlated mechanical motion of multiple gears. However, the realization of molecular-level 2D gearbox machinery with correlated motion among multiple units remains highly challenging. Here, we report a molecular-level 2D gearbox in a crystal, formed through the supramolecular assembly of an Au(I)-complex rotor with tripodal triptycene and triadamantyl phosphine (Ad 3 P) rotators, connected via an ethynyl–Au(I) unit. Upon heating, the rotators within a 2D hexagonal gear network exhibit 120° site-exchange rotational motion in a correlated manner, as revealed by single-crystal X-ray diffraction (XRD), 2 H solid-state (SS) NMR spectroscopy, and time-resolved variable-temperature XRD measurements. In addition, density functional theory calculations provide insight into the energetic preference for correlated motion within the gear-network. This 2D intermolecular gearbox in the crystalline state represents a supramolecular platform in which the intermolecular gearing motion has a large impact on the bulk crystal, which could provide a bridge between molecular-level mechanical properties and macroscale SS physical functions.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: A two-dimensional molecular gearbox operated in a crystalline solid

abstract: Bacteria in the genus Yersinia use type III secretion to inject several effectors into phagocytes to disrupt signaling. Two effectors disrupt host signaling by inactivation of RhoA, triggering pyrin inflammasome assembly in infected phagocytes and protective immunity. A third protein, YopM, counteracts effector-triggered immunity by binding to and inactivating pyrin. Prior evidence suggested that gain of function codon changes in the pyrin gene MEFV that cause Familial Mediterranean Fever (FMF) and provide resistance to Yersinia pestis were selected to evade YopM binding. YopM was shown to bind an N-terminal region of human pyrin, which includes the eponymous pyrin domain (PYD), however, the interaction mechanism was undefined. Using bacterial two-hybrid assay, protein biochemistry, and X-ray crystallography, we determined that YopM binds to the PYD, which has few validated FMF amino acid variants. We show that YopM binds PYD R42, a “Site 2” amino acid important for positive and negative regulation of pyrin and that binding to the R42W variant is reduced. YopM amino acid change variants defective for PYD binding failed to inhibit the pyrin inflammasome in human monocytes infected with Yersinia. In addition, PYD binding was dispensable for YopM to inhibit the inflammasome in murine macrophages, suggesting this effector uses a distinct mechanism to target mouse pyrin. These results define that Y. pestis YopM binds to human PYD to promote pathogenesis, and because Site 2 variants that evade YopM binding have low gain of function inflammasome activity, these data may explain why most validated FMF codon changes are in other domains of pyrin.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: The Yersinia pestis effector YopM binds the human pyrin death domain to inhibit inflammasome activation and effector-triggered immunity

abstract: Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond are a versatile quantum sensing platform for high sensitivity measurements of magnetic fields, temperature, and strain with nanoscale spatial resolution. A common bottleneck is the analysis of optically detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) spectra, where target quantities are encoded in resonance features. Conventional nonlinear fitting is often computationally expensive, sensitive to initialization, and prone to failure at low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Here we introduce a robust, efficient machine learning (ML) framework for real-time ODMR analysis based on a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN). The model performs direct parameter inference without initial guesses or iterative optimization, and is naturally parallelizable on graphics processing units (GPU) for high-throughput processing. We validate the approach on both synthetic and experimental datasets, showing improved throughput, accuracy, and robustness than standard nonlinear fitting, with the largest gains in the low-SNR regime. We further validate our methods in two representative sensing applications: diagnosing intracellular temperature changes using nanodiamond probes and widefield magnetic imaging of superconducting vortices in a high-temperature superconductor. This deep-learning inference framework enables fast and reliable extraction of physical parameters from complex ODMR data and provides a scalable route to real-time quantum sensing and imaging.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: A deep-learning-boosted framework for quantum sensing with nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond

abstract: Electrical communication between excitable cells depends on gap junction (GJ) currents and field-mediated ephaptic interactions, but their relative contributions have been difficult to quantify, limiting insight into arrhythmia and other disorders of bioelectric signaling. Building on the nanoscale, sodium channel-rich perinexus at the cardiac intercalated disc, we developed a “Single-on-Paired” (SoP) preparation, recording whole-cell sodium current from one adult ventricular myocyte that remains coupled by an intercalated disc to an intact partner. This revealed a composite two-cell sodium current with two rising-phase slopes and an activation jump between closely spaced voltage steps, an “Intercalated Disc Signature” (IDS) absent from isolated single myocytes and providing a direct readout of intercellular activation. Rapid sodium channel activation cannot be resolved under voltage clamp at physiological extracellular sodium ([Na +] o), so SoP recordings used reduced [Na +] o of 25 to 35 mM. Within this nonphysiologic range, graded GJ inhibition, perinexal widening with an Scn1b-derived competitive adhesion peptide, and [Na +] o modulation showed that GJ inhibition abolished the IDS at 25 mM, whereas a modest 10 mM rise to 35 mM restored it despite persistent GJ inhibition. GJ coupling and a perinexus-centered ephaptic mechanism are thus separable contributors to intercellular activation whose relative engagement is set by extracellular sodium. A two-cell computational model constrained by these data reproduces the IDS and predicts that at physiological 145 mM [Na +] o with reduced GJ conductance, perinexus-centered ephaptic mechanisms suffice for intercellular activation. Clamping cleft potential, but not cleft sodium, disrupts this behavior in silico, identifying cleft potential as the proximal ephaptic signal.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: A nanoscale gap junction–perinexus nanodomain governs balance of ephaptic and gap-junctional activation in excitable cell pairs

abstract: Defective Fas cell surface death receptor (FAS) signaling leads to lymphoproliferative and autoimmune disorder, yet the mechanisms involved remain unclear. Using genetic mouse models homozygous for the lymphoproliferation spontaneous mutation (Fas lpr), we showed that age-associated B cells (ABCs) were critical drivers of lymphadenopathy and autoimmunity. Single-cell transcriptomics of lymph node immune cells in Fas lpr mice revealed a marked expansion of ABCs. Depletion of these ABCs in Fas lpr mice significantly restrained lymph node enlargement and alleviated autoimmune manifestations, whereas adoptive transfer of ABCs from Fas lpr mice to wild-type mice exacerbated disease pathology. Mechanistically, p38α signaling emerged as a critical regulator of ABC differentiation and function, and conditional deletion of p38α in CD11c + cells profoundly suppressed ABC expansion and ameliorated autoimmune manifestations in Fas lpr mice. Furthermore, we identified CXCL10 as an important downstream effector of p38α signaling in ABCs that drives autoimmune disorder. Neutralization of CXCL10 significantly attenuated disease severity in Fas lpr mice. Although clinical relevance analyses of autoimmune patient cohorts revealed a parallel expansion of ABCs in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and primary Sjögren’s syndrome, ABCs with higher p38α content were specifically enriched in SLE patients. Together, these findings identify p38α-driven ABCs as an important regulator of lymphoproliferative and autoimmune disorder in Fas lpr mice and suggest that targeting the p38α−CXCL10 axis in ABCs may be a therapeutic strategy for treating this autoimmune disease.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Age-associated B cells drive lymphoproliferative and autoimmune disorder in Fas lpr mice through the p38α−CXCL10 signaling axis

abstract: Nematic liquid crystals can dramatically reconfigure under dynamic forcing, providing exciting opportunities in active matter. Here, we study a disk colloid with hybrid planar and homeotropic anchoring rotated by an external magnetic field which generates a dynamic companion topological defect. The disk moves faster when the defect sweeps across the disk’s face. We identify the defect as a nonsingular twist wall, characterize the twist energy landscape, and identify that the sweeping motion is driven by a topological instability. As the defect sweeps, it reverses the handedness of twist and lowers the free energy in the fluid in the gap above the disk. Landau–de Gennes modeling shows that the sweeping wall behaves as a propagating director texture: the director field is nearly stationary in the wall frame, while nematogens rotate locally as the wall passes. The nematogens’ rotation generates a viscous stress on the surface of the disk that hastens its propulsion. Thus, the defect acts as a flagellum that powers colloid swimming, providing an example of a dissipative topological structure whose dynamics can be harnessed to perform useful work.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: A sweeping twist defect as a topological flagellum that enhances colloid translation

abstract: Formation and rupture of vesicles are fundamental processes underlying diverse phenomena in biology, materials science, and biomedical applications. Vesicles form when the area of a growing disk-like membrane reaches the instability point at which the energy barrier to the disk-to-vesicle transition vanishes. Observing such topological transitions in lipid bilayers is a challenge because of their nanoscale dimensions and rapid dynamics. We study a scaled-up model of membranes assembled from rod-shaped colloidal particles. The unique features of colloidal membranes enable the real-time visualization of spontaneous vesicle closure driven by an instability arising from competition between edge and bending energies that is universal to all membrane-based materials. A continuum theory with independently measured material parameters quantitatively predicts the instability point for vesicle formation and intermediate membrane conformations during the disk-to-vesicle transition. The instability generates monodisperse, selectively permeable colloidosomes whose size is controlled by gravity and membrane elasticity, providing a scalable and programmable platform for diverse applications.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Mechanical instability generates monodisperse colloidosomes

abstract: The polymer–nanoparticle interphase is essential for fabricating high-performance nanocomposites, as it dictates mechanical properties through interfacial stress transfer and energy dissipation. However, engineering the buried interphases remains challenging due to the complex hierarchical structure and methodological limitations, particularly in silica–rubber systems where confined polymer chain conformation and hydrogen-bond dynamics are poorly resolved. Herein, a selective polymer-removal technique was developed to strip free and loosely bound polymer under extreme conditions, enabling TEM visualization of polymer chain-like interfacial features consistent with train-, loop-, and tail-like adsorption motifs in silica/silicone rubber nanocomposites. Correlative analysis combining STEM-EELS, high-resolution NMR, in situ variable-temperature IR, and 2D low-field NMR spectroscopy resolves hydrogen bonding between silica surface hydroxyls and silicone backbone oxygen atoms (Si-O-H···O-Si), which exhibit temperature-dependent behavior. Quantitative analysis reveals the strategic modulation of interphase layer thickness: As the apparent hydroxyl density of silica varied from 2.1 to 12.9 OH nm −2, the interphase thickness increased from 4.1 ± 0.8 nm to 13.2 ± 1.4 nm (9.5 mol% polymer phenyl); increasing the polymer phenyl content to 29.7 mol% further expands the layer to 23.4 ± 1.0 nm. Molecular dynamics simulations also suggest that higher silica surface hydroxyl density enhances multipoint adsorption of polymer chain, which promotes the formation of loop and train conformations. These confined chain arrangements are consistent with the reduced Arrhenius activation energy from 101 to 50 kJ mol −1 measured by dynamic rheology, which facilitates interfacial chain mobility and hydrogen-bond exchange during deformation. These findings provide molecular-level insights for the rational design of polymer nanocomposites.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Modulating chain conformations and hydrogen-bond dynamics at silica–rubber interfaces for enhanced energy dissipation in composites

abstract: Self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) serve as effective hole-transport layers (HTLs) in perovskite solar cells (PSCs), facilitating energy-level alignment and defect passivation at perovskite interfaces. However, their integration is limited by weak anchoring to transparent conducting oxides (TCOs), resulting in desorption during deposition and the release of acidic protons, which react with components of the perovskite leading to degradation [T. Li et al., Nature 648, 84–90 (2025) and C. Fei et al., Science 391, eadz7969 (2026)]. To strengthen anchoring between the SAM and TCO while simultaneously mitigating proton-induced degradation of the perovskite, we have prepared ionic SAMs featuring a phosphonate anchoring group and a perovskite-compatible cation. The benchmark SAMs, [2-(3,6-dimethoxy-9 H -carbazol-9-yl)ethyl]phosphonic acid (MeO-2PACz) for tin-based PSCs and [4-(3,6-dimethyl-9H-carbazol-9-yl)butyl]phosphonic acid (Me-4PACz) for lead-based PSCs, were reacted with formamidine, generated in situ via precipitation of KCl from formamidinium chloride (FACl) and KOH, to afford [FA] + [MeO-2PACz] − and [FA] + [Me-4PACz] −, respectively. After thermal aging at 65 °C in a N 2 atmosphere for 10 h, the [FA] + [MeO-2PACz] − -based device retained approximately 85% of its initial power conversion efficiency (PCE), compared with only 65% for the MeO-2PACz-based device, demonstrating enhanced thermal stability. Using [FA] + [Me-4PACz] − as the HTL in lead-based PSCs results in devices with a PCE of 26.53%, outperforming the PCE of 24.97% for the Me-4PACz-based device. After heating at 85°C for over 1,000 h, the [FA] + [Me-4PACz] − -based device retained ca. 88% of its initial efficiency. This study establishes the broad utility of ionic SAMs as versatile compounds to concurrently increase device efficiency and long-term stability.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Design of ionic self-assembled monolayers suppressing proton release to mitigate proton-based degradation of perovskite solar cells

abstract: Ice-nucleating particles (INPs) play a critical role in regulating glaciation and precipitation formation in mixed-phase cloud (containing liquid and ice), yet their spatial variability across different scales remains poorly constrained. In this study, coordinated immersion freezing INP measurements from multiple sites during two campaigns in an urban–rural environment and complex mountainous terrain were used to investigate INP spatial distributions at tens-of-kilometer scales. At these scales, INP concentrations were generally spatially homogeneous during each campaign, indicating that single-site measurements can often represent surrounding areas. Occasional spatial differences were observed at warm activation temperatures (higher than −20 °C), ascribed to variations in heat-labile, likely biological INPs. Extending the analysis to the synoptic scale across multiple campaigns, warm-temperature INPs showed greater site-to-site differences, suggesting stronger influences from local or regional sources. In contrast, INPs active at colder temperatures showed much stronger spatial similarity between two inland continental sites separated by 800 km, revealing a broader regional coherence in this INP population. This was also observed at the coastal site, but only under continental air mass influence; the similarity weakened under marine air masses. These results suggest that cold-temperature INPs may reflect a broader INP background over continents such as that contributed by windblown dust. Our findings provide direct observational constraints on the representativeness of single-site INP measurements, which can help inform the strategy for representing variations in INP populations in atmospheric models.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Contrasting spatial homogeneity in atmospheric ice-nucleating particles from local to synoptic scales

abstract: Evolutionary game theory and ecological coexistence theory both seek to predict the outcome of competition between biological entities, be they strategies or species, but the two fields have relied on largely separate approaches. Replicator equations provide a foundation for predicting the outcome of strategic competition, but comparing how different mechanisms alter competition across games remains challenging. Inspired by modern coexistence theory from community ecology, we develop Strategic Coexistence Theory (SCT), which translates payoff-based invasion conditions at monomorphic boundary conditions into strategic niche differences and fitness differences between any two competing strategies described by classic replicator dynamics. We show that SCT recovers the classic classification of two-strategy games and also allows us to compare mechanisms for the evolution of cooperation within a shared niche-fitness difference space. In stochastic games, environmental stochasticity increases both boundary invasion growth rates, whereas in multiplayer public-goods games, nonlinear benefits can either stabilize or destabilize competition. These applications also show that the number or stability of internal equilibria generally cannot be predicted from invasion growth rates at monomorphic boundaries, illustrating a key limitation of characterizing competitive systems using boundary invasion rates alone. Together, these results show that SCT provides a coexistence-theoretic perspective for characterizing how different mechanisms alter strategy competition across games.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Strategic coexistence theory for evolutionary games

abstract: Earthquakes propagating faster than the shear wave-speed are commonly thought to undergo a supershear transition upon which they discontinuously jump from the sub-Rayleigh regime to the supershear one. The super-Rayleigh regime, i.e., the range of propagation speeds between the Rayleigh and shear wave-speeds, is regarded as “forbidden” by the two-dimensional classical rupture theory. Here, we revisit the assumptions underlying the classical theory and develop a rupture theory that takes into account the dependence of the fault strength (frictional resistance) on the slip rate. The theory quantitatively agrees with numerical simulations nearly up to the Rayleigh wave-speed. Yet, very close to the latter, numerical rupture solutions change their character due to frictional rate nonlinearity, involving rate-strengthening friction, and rupture continuously propagates through the “forbidden” super-Rayleigh range into the supershear regime, without a sharp supershear transition. These results demonstrate that frictional rate dependence, generically observed in experiments, can have profound implications for fast earthquake propagation.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Breakdown of the classical rupture theory and earthquake propagation in the “forbidden” super-Rayleigh range

abstract: Like plant toxins, synthetic insecticides can exert strong selective pressures on pest populations. While responses to both plant toxins and synthetic insecticides can depend on adaptive changes in the nuclear genotype of the pest species, increasing evidence suggests that symbiotic microbes, particularly gut microbes, can also influence these responses. In the cotton bollworm, Helicoverpa armigera, concentrations of the symbiont Corynebacterium glyciniphilum increased in moth strains that were treated with the pyrethroid pesticide lambda-cyhalothrin (LCH), and they were also high in LCH-resistant strains and in populations exposed to 2-Tridecanone (2-TD), a secondary defense compound that is present in the Solanaceae. This increase enhanced the ability of H. armigera to overcome not only the pesticide but also a key defense mechanism in the solanaceous plants. In field populations of H. armigera, the abundance of C. glyciniphilum was lowest in populations feeding on nonsolanaceous plants that were sensitive to LCH. Based on gene knockouts, the underlying reason for the enhanced defensive capability provided by C. glyciniphilum was attributed to two detoxification enzyme genes (a P450 cytochrome and an esterase) which can metabolize both LCH and 2-TD into nontoxic degradation products. These findings suggest that a common mechanism mediated by a symbiont contributes to the insect’s capacity to develop resistance to both a pesticide and a host plant toxin.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
journal_ref: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
title: Pyrethroid insecticide exposure enhances the ability of Helicoverpa armigera to counter host plant defenses through symbiotic bacteria

abstract: Understanding the origin of fast ionic transport in solids remains challenging due to the complex interplay between structural changes and ionic motion, particularly across superionic transitions (SITs). These transitions are commonly viewed as concurrent evolution of the host framework and the mobile sublattice. However, using Li3InBr6 as a model superionic conductor (SIC), we show that the two subsystems are instead sequentially activated upon thermal stimulation. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations reveal that heating first induces a threshold-driven, collective framework distortion (at 290 K) which is associated with the flattened potential energy surface (PES), while Li+ diffusion emerges only after additional thermal activation (at 310 K) and subsequently evolves from anisotropic to three-dimensional (3D) diffusion. The resulting delay gives rise to an intermediate state, where pronounced framework distortion coexists with solid-like Li+ dynamics. Our findings provide new insights into the structure–property relationships governing solid-state diffusion and suggest a transferable design principle for high-performance SICs.
title: Delayed transport response during superionic transition of lithium-ion conductors

abstract: Efficient integrated quantum memories are a key enabling technology for scalable quantum networks and photonic quantum processors, yet their efficiencies have remained below the critical threshold of 90% required for demanding applications. Here we demonstrate an integrated photonic quantum memory with a storage-and-retrieval efficiency of 90.2(4)% for single-photon-level weak coherent pulses and a storage fidelity of 99.3(1)% for time-bin qubits, using a waveguide cavity fabricated in Pr 3 + : Y 2 S i O 5 . This performance is enabled by the high absorption-to-loss ratio of Pr 3 + ions in a low-loss waveguide cavity, combined with a time-reversal technique to overcome the dispersion-limited cavity linewidth and a novel spectral preparation scheme that creates a clean transparency window while utilizing a single class of ions that is compatible for spin-wave storage. Our results establish the first integrated photonic memory beyond the 90% efficiency threshold, representing an important step toward applications that demand the highest performance, such as scalable quantum repeaters, photonic quantum computing and device-independent quantum key distribution.
title: Efficient Integrated Quantum Memory Based on a Waveguide Cavity

abstract: We investigate the emergence of an amplitude (Higgs-like) mode in the gapless phase of the (1+1)D XXZ spin chain. Unlike in conventional settings, where amplitude modes arise from spontaneous symmetry breaking, here we identify a symmetry-preserving underdamped excitation above a Luttinger-liquid ground state without long-range order. Using nonequilibrium quench spectroscopy, we demonstrate that this mode manifests as oscillations of U(1)-symmetric observables following a sudden quench. At the free-fermion point, we show that the mode, although embedded in a gapless continuum, remains underdamped because its spectral weight is concentrated by Van Hove singularities of the zero-momentum multiparticle spectrum. By combining numerical simulations with Bethe-ansatz analyses, we trace its microscopic origin in the interacting chain to a specific family of excitations. We further discuss experimental pathways to detect this mode in easy-plane quantum magnets and programmable quantum simulators. Our results showcase quantum quenches as a powerful tool for probing collective excitations beyond the reach of conventional linear-response measurements.
title: Quench spectroscopy of amplitude modes in a one-dimensional critical phase

abstract: Understanding how protons and neutrons are located differently in an atomic nucleus can provide fundamental information on nuclear structure and have far-reaching implications for astrophysics. A precise determination of this important difference, often quantified by the so-called neutron skin thickness, is challenging both theoretically and experimentally. Here we show a category of observables in heavy-ion collisions could directly access the neutron skin by leveraging extreme collision geometries. In super-central collisions, the neutrons in the skin have an appreciable probability of missing the bulk collisions and flying down the collision beam pipeline, thus becoming countable by dedicated detectors there. In peripheral collisions, the nucleons in the overlapping collision zone are dominantly from the neutron skin and induce a measurable isospin asymmetry. These observables are demonstrated by quantitative simulations to have robust sensitivity for constraining the thickness of both 208 Pb and 48 Ca nuclei. The asymmetric collision between 48 Ca and 40 Ca nuclei is found to be a unique and powerful way for probing the neutron skin.
title: Probing the neutron skin with extreme collision geometries in heavy-ion collisions

abstract: Moir'e superlattices produced by the superposition of twisted sublattices have emerged as a powerful platform for engineering correlated phases, band topology, and localization of excitations, yet their realization is often hindered by the extreme sensitivity of system properties to twist angle. Here, we demonstrate that magic' moiré physics can be accessed in two-dimensional non-separable lattices produced by sublattices that are untwisted, but feature mismatched lattice constants. Using the optical induction technique, we experimentally realize reconfigurable non-separable moiré lattices where the transition between commensurable and incommensurable phases is controlled by the ratio of sublattice constants. We report the first observation of a localization-delocalization transition (LDT) in a two-dimensional quasiperiodic system with incommensurate periods along both spatial directions, where the transition is determined by sublattice amplitudes and occurs around magic’ ratios of sublattice constants, and the underlying physics is revealed to be governed by a flat-band mechanism. These results establish relative spatial scale of sublattices as a control parameter for localization in a nonseparable two-dimensional quasiperiodic system, providing an experimentally accessible setting for studying localization beyond the separable Aubry–André limit.
title: Observation of light localization in untwisted two-dimensional moiré photonic lattices

abstract: Using a direct scan of 26 energy points near the J / ψ resonance, we perform the first measurement of the relative phase ϕ γ, 3 g between the strong and electromagnetic amplitudes in J / ψ → K ¯ 0 K * (892) 0 + c. c. and J / ψ → K + K * (892) − + c. c. Unexpectedly, the phase in the neutral channel is found to be ∼ 15 0 °, deviating from orthogonality (90°) by 4.8 σ and from a relative real amplitude (0° or 180°) by 12.6 σ or 2.8 σ, respectively. By contrast, the charged channel phase is consistent with ∼ 180 ° within 1 σ, exhibiting channel-dependent behavior. The corresponding branching fractions are consistent with the world averages but achieve better than twofold improvement in precision. The ratios between the branching fractions of J / ψ → K ¯ 0 K * (892) 0 + c. c. and J / ψ → K + K * (892) − + c. c.
title: Unexpected Large Relative Strong Phase and Search for Isospin Breaking and C P Asymmetries in J / ψ → K * (892) K ¯

abstract: The Unruh effect predicts that accelerated observers perceive the inertial vacuum as populated by particles, providing a flat-spacetime analogue of Hawking radiation. Its direct observation, however, remains experimentally challenging, since an Unruh temperature of 1 K requires accelerations of order 10 20 m / s 2 . Here, we show that the relative Lamb shift–the radiative correction to the atomic transition frequency–of a centripetally accelerated atom inside a high- Q cavity provides a sensitive spectroscopic probe of the Unruh effect at dramatically lower accelerations. The cavity reshapes the electromagnetic density of states and converts otherwise tiny noninertial corrections into tunable spectroscopic shifts. Depending on the orbital parameters and cavity detuning, these corrections can enhance or suppress the total relative Lamb shift, producing strong quenching and even complete screening. For experimentally motivated atomic, orbital, and cavity parameters, we predict a rotation-induced frequency correction of order 1 k H z at accelerations of order 10 4 m / s 2 , about 16 orders of magnitude below the acceleration corresponding to a linear Unruh temperature of 1 K . These results identify cavity-controlled Lamb-shift spectroscopy as a promising route toward laboratory tests of the circular Unruh effect at experimentally accessible acceleration scales.
title: Probing the circular Unruh effect with cavity-controlled Lamb shifts

abstract: The complex eigenvalues of Markov generators govern oscillatory properties of relaxation, autocorrelation, and linear response. We show that these eigenvalues are localized by nonequilibrium cycles of the generator, thus revealing a fundamental tradeoff between thermodynamic driving, oscillation, and decay of eigenmodes. Specifically, we prove that each complex eigenvalue is confined to a region determined by the cycle affinity and the eigenvector "winding number" of some nonequilibrium cycle. In discrete and continuous unicyclic systems, we also demonstrate that the winding number is determined by the ordered eigenvalue index, yielding new thermodynamic bounds on the slowest and fastest relaxation modes. In discrete multicyclic systems, our approach unifies and extends several previous inequalities and proves the Uhl–Seifert ellipse conjecture.
title: Cycle affinity and winding localize eigenvalues of Markov generators

abstract: The presence of a dissipative environment substantially disrupts unitary evolution. Nevertheless, key features of the evolution, such as its integrable or chaotic nature, are not immediately erased by dissipation. To understand this, we model environment-induced dissipation as a convex combination of unitary evolution and a random Kraus map, and examine how signatures of integrability gradually fade with increasing dissipation strength. Our analysis shows that in the weakly dissipative regime, the complex eigenvalue spectrum organizes into well-defined, high-density clusters. We estimate the critical dissipation threshold beyond which these clusters disappear, rendering the dynamics indistinguishable from chaotic evolution. This threshold depends only on the number of spectral clusters and the rank of the Kraus map. To characterize this transition, we introduce the eigenvalue angular velocity as a diagnostic of integrability loss. We illustrate our findings using several integrable quantum circuits, including the dissipative quantum Fourier transform. Our results provide a quantitative picture of how noise gradually erases the footprints of unitary integrability in open quantum systems.
title: Dissipation-induced threshold on integrability footprints

abstract: We predict a fundamentally new superconducting state in superconductor/antiferromagnet heterostructures with Ising spin–orbit coupling: proximity-induced orbital antiferromagnetism. In this state, the order parameter acquires a periodic phase modulation locked to the magnetic lattice, generating atomic-scale loop currents with opposite orbital moments on neighboring unit cells. Its emergence requires at least three nonequivalent magnetic sublattices per unit cell and finite spin–orbit coupling. Using NbSe 2 /MnPS 3 as a concrete example, we combine first-principles and Bogoliubov–de Gennes calculations to demonstrate that the proximity-induced exchange field leads to robust phase modulation. Unlike FFLO and helical states, the phase gradient is atomic-scale, the state is current-carrying, and it remains uniquely stable over the full parameter range. The state manifests as characteristic finite-energy dips in the electronic density of states, accessible by tunneling spectroscopy, including STM.
title: Proximity-induced orbital antiferromagnetism in Ising superconductors

abstract: Interacting quantum many-body systems can rapidly scramble quantum information, raising the question of how precisely local subsystems can track the passage of time during this evolution. In this work, we develop a quantum metrological framework for quantum chaos by showing that local subsystems of information scrambling systems naturally function as quantum stopwatches. The reduced quantum state of a subsystem encodes the passage of time through its local temporal distinguishability along its dynamical trajectory. Treating time as the estimation parameter, we then derive a generalized quantum Cramer-Rao bound that directly relates the precision of time estimation to the decay of out-of-time ordered correlators (OTOCs) and subsystem quantum Fisher information (QFI). For a single qubit subsystem, we obtain an exact relation between the incoherent component of subsystem QFI and the decay rate of OTOCs in quantumly chaotic dynamics, while the total subsystem QFI provides an upper bound to the corresponding decay rate. Furthermore, using a scaling analysis based on imaginary-time correlators, we investigate under what conditions the incoherent subsystem QFI exhibits critical amplification near quantum phase transitions. Our results are demonstrated and verified by a numerical analysis of the dynamics of a chaotic Ising chain.
title: Quantum timekeeping and the dynamics of scrambling in critical systems

abstract: Spectroscopy of muonic atoms is, to date, the most accurate technique to extract parameters of the nuclear charge density. The same reasons for their heightened sensitivity to nuclear parameters, a large overlap of the muonic wavefunction with the nucleus, makes them attractive systems to test Beyond the Standard Model (BSM) Physics. This raises concerns of self-consistency as the same data are used to, first, extract nuclear parameters, and second, check the consistency with BSM models. We combine the two steps and self-consistently extract the nuclear and BSM parameters. We show that the data are consistent with vanishing BSM coupling and extract robust exclusion bounds. We further note that the nuclear parameters change under the influence of those BSM couplings on the parameter fits and compare with the fit solely based on quantum electrodynamics (QED).
title: Self-consistent bounds on beyond the Standard Model bosons from spectroscopy of muonic atoms with magic nuclei

abstract: Natural birefringent crystals suffer from weak optical anisotropy, which limits polarization separation and hinders device miniaturization. Here, we demonstrate meta-crystals that exhibit ultrabroadband extreme birefringence, enabling the angular separation between ordinary and extraordinary rays to approach 180° with near-unity transmission in an ultrathin geometry. This unprecedented performance stems from the engineering of anisotropic dispersion and a reciprocity-protected anomalous Brewster condition that suppresses reflection across a broad spectrum. Orthogonally polarized beams are separated within a small fraction of the propagation length required by conventional birefringent materials, as experimentally validated through a tunable meta-crystal. Such efficient, wavelength-scale polarization separation enables compact and reconfigurable meta-devices with multifunctionality, including waveplates, absorptive polarizers, arbitrary-angle polarization beam splitters, and polarization-dependent wavefront modulators. These results establish meta-crystals as a class of highly efficient, ultrathin birefringent media, promising transformative advances in integrated polarization optics from microwave to optical frequencies.
title: Extreme birefringence in meta-crystals

abstract: We uncover a mechanism for far-from-equilibrium topological phase transitions, via a one-dimensional compact phase model evolving deterministically from random initial conditions. It rests on topology and symmetry rather than on phenomenological postulates: phase compactness permits vortices, and a homogeneous fixed point suppresses their nucleation, with the fixed point itself implied by phase-shift symmetry. The competition between vortex-induced disordering and relaxation toward homogeneity drives a continuous nonequilibrium transition, whose universality class we identify as directed percolation (DP). We demonstrate this by constructing the corresponding effective field theory and numerically confirming DP critical scaling through dynamical-scaling analysis.
title: Far-from-equilibrium topological phase transition in one dimension

abstract: The theory of bremsstrahlung e → e γ by extremely high energy electrons passing through ordinary matter has been qualitatively incomplete. We revisit the suppression of bremsstrahlung by the Landau-Pomeranchuk-Migdal effect, here accounting for quantum disruption of that effect from pair production. Our analysis covers the full range of ultrarelativistic electron and photon energies (subject to a few simplifying approximations).
title: Extremely High-Energy Bremsstrahlung in Matter

abstract: We report the observation of dispersive spin excitons in the rare-earth magnetic Weyl semimetal NdAlSi through comprehensive thermodynamic and inelastic neutron scattering measurements. Notably, the behavior of spin excitons is strongly modulated by magnetic order: they remain dispersive in the paramagnetic phase, shift to higher energies and broaden in the incommensurate antiferromagnetic phase, and split into distinct branches in the commensurate ferrimagnetic phase. To elucidate the microscopic origin of this evolution, we construct an effective crystal electric field (CEF)–exchange model and calculate the excitation spectra within the random-phase approximation. This framework consistently accounts for the observed excitation dispersions and mode splitting by incorporating two magnetic-order-dependent effects: an effective renormalization of the local CEF environment associated with the concomitant reconstruction of the itinerant electronic structure across the magnetic phases, and exchange-generated molecular fields that lift the Kramers degeneracy. Our findings reveal the interplay among localized 4f states, itinerant electrons, and magnetic order, and establish NdAlSi as a model platform for studying collective CEF excitations in rare-earth quantum materials.
title: Spin Excitons Modulated by Magnetic Orders in a Magnetic Weyl Semimetal NdAlSi

abstract: Here, we present direct, time-resolved measurements of resonant wave–particle interactions during strong guide-field magnetic reconnection in the PHAse Space MApping (PHASMA) experiment. Correlated measurements of lower-hybrid drift waves (LHDWs) and electron velocity distribution functions (EVDFs), obtained from reproducible reconnection discharges, reveal that coherent finite- k ∥ LHDWs develop at the reconnection separatrix and produce discrete velocity-space enhancements within the thermal electron population at velocities matching the measured parallel phase velocities, v_{ph}=omega/k_{}. As the wave activity saturates and decays, these resonant structures broaden into plateaus on a timescale of ~2 microsecond, in quantitative agreement with the quasilinear relaxation time independently inferred from the measured wave amplitudes, coherence times, and plateau widths. These measurements establish a direct experimental link between lower-hybrid wave activity and resonant electron energization during magnetic reconnection, identifying a kinetic pathway for magnetic-energy conversion.
title: Kinetic Pathway for Electron Energization during Strong Guide-Field Magnetic Reconnection

abstract: Chiroptical effects using circularly polarized light in isotropic media produce signals that change sign when switching either molecular handedness (enantio-sensitivity) or the light helicity (circular dichroism). Here, we break this enantio-sensitive-and-dichroic paradigm by measuring a new type of chiroptical signal which is enantio-sensitive but not dichroic. We photoionize chiral molecules using femtosecond laser pulses and detect the three-dimensional photoelectron momentum distribution. The non-dichroic, enantio-sensitive asymmetry is encoded in octupolar and higher multipolar terms in the photoelectron angular distribution, which appear in multiphoton or strong-field ionization with elliptically polarized fields or cross polarized two-color fields. The robustness of the enantio-sensitivity with respect to the relative phase between the vectorial components of the ionizing field represents an example of symmetry protection, and opens unexplored opportunities for imaging ultrafast dynamics in chiral molecules, such as enantio-sensitive photoelectron spectroscopy with bright squeezed vacuum states.
title: Nondichroic enantio-sensitive chiroptical spectroscopy in isotropic media

abstract: Giant piezoelectricity in ferroelectrics is commonly associated with phase-boundary instabilities, among which the polymorphic phase boundary (PPB) is a prominent example conventionally attributed to the coexistence of ferroelectric phases. Here, using large-scale molecular dynamics simulations of the lead-free (K,Na)NbO 3 –(Bi,Na)ZrO 3 solid solutions, we show that the PPB hosts a percolating multifractal polar domain which governs the dielectric and piezoelectric responses. By quantifying the global fractal dimension and multifractal spectrum width of this polar network, we identify fractal connectivity and multiscale heterogeneity as geometric descriptors for the PPB. The maximum reversible piezoelectric response occurs at an intermediate fractal-domain volume fraction, where the fractal backbone preserves polar memory and provides the restoring force required for reversibility while the surrounding nonfractal regions supply the polar compliance needed for large polarization rotation and strain. The theoretical piezoelectric coefficient represents a single-crystal upper limit, whereas ceramic measurements average over grain orientations and may include irreversible contributions. These results establish percolating multifractal polar domains as a microscopic mechanism for PPB-enhanced piezoelectricity and suggest fractal connectivity as a design parameter for high-performance piezoelectrics.
title: Percolating multifractal domains at polymorphic phase boundary
